in_context.text: This verse sits in a section on prayer and conduct in worship (2:1-15). Paul has told men to pray without anger (2:8) and women to dress modestly and learn quietly (2:9-11). He then gives reasons from Adam and Eve (2:13-14).

speaker.text: The letter names Paul the apostle as its writer. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote it in his name, while others defend Paul's authorship.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: Women and men in the church's gatherings for worship and teaching.

what.text: Paul says he does not permit a woman to teach or to have authority over a man, but to be in quietness. The next verses give his reasons: Adam was formed first, and Eve was deceived.

events.text: Paul gives this instruction while Timothy is leading the church in Ephesus. False teaching from within was troubling the church then.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110.

where.text: The instruction is for the church in Ephesus, a wealthy port city known for its temple of Artemis. The letter does not say where it was written, though Paul may have been in Macedonia.

purpose.text: The letter guides how believers should conduct themselves in worship and in the household of God. It also aims to counter false teachers.

big_picture.text: The chapter opens with prayer for all people, because God wants all to be saved (2:1-4). The rules for worship that follow serve a quiet, godly common life.

for_readers.text: Readers should notice that this is about order in the church's worship and teaching. They should also see that Paul ties his instruction to the creation account.

misuse.popular_reading: Quoted as a blanket rule that women should never speak, lead, or teach in any setting, or as proof that the Bible looks down on women.

in_context_reading.text: The verse belongs to instructions on prayer and conduct in the church's worship (2:1-15; 3:14-15). The same passage also tells women to learn (2:11). How far it applies today is debated among Christians.

christians_differ.text: One view, often called complementarian, holds that this is a lasting rule: certain teaching and leading roles over men in the church are reserved for men, because Paul grounds it in creation order (2:13). Another view, often called egalitarian, reads it as aimed at a specific problem with false teaching in Ephesus, and points to the rare word for authority. Many churches hold positions between these.

why_it_matters.text: This verb, authentein, appears only here in the New Testament. The lexicon glosses it as "to domineer" and "to govern, exercise authority over." Its exact shade of meaning is part of why readers disagree about the verse.
The word means quietness, stillness, or silence. The lexicon places this verse under the sense "stillness, silence"; in 2 Thessalonians 3:12 the same word means a quiet way of life.
Anēr can mean "man" or "husband." The lexicon lists this verse under "man" as opposed to woman, though some readers take it as husband and wife.

takeaway.text: This verse gives Paul's instruction on order in worship at Ephesus, grounded in his reading of creation. It should be read with the whole passage and the letter's purpose, keeping in mind that Christians differ on how it applies today.

resolved.reason: The lexicon lists 1 Timothy 2:11-12 under sense 2, 'stillness, silence,' not under the 'quietness' sense used for 2 Thessalonians 3:12. Using 2 Thessalonians to argue that the word here need not mean silence goes against the cited source's own classification of this verse.
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources
